caption:
Optical imagery needs a clear sky. Radar does not.

An optical sensor collects visible light, the same way a camera does. Cloud cover blocks that light entirely. During West Africa's rainy season, when flood risk and ground activity both peak, large parts of the region sit under cloud for weeks. An optical pass over a clouded area returns a picture of the cloud, not the ground.

Synthetic-aperture radar sends its own microwave signal and reads the return. That wavelength passes through cloud and most rain. The image comes back regardless of weather. This is why radar, not optical, carries the load for flood-plain and infrastructure monitoring in this region — the months you need coverage most are the months optical is least usable.

The trade: radar imagery takes more work to interpret. It shows surface roughness and moisture, not color and shape. Reading it well is a separate skill from reading a photograph.
